title: Where was Agade, the capital of the Sargonic empire?
short: The city from which Sargon and his successors ruled Mesopotamia c. 2300 BCE has never been securely located, despite more than a century of searching in central Iraq.
matters: Agade was the political centre of the first territorial state in Mesopotamia, and its archives, workshops and temple of Ishtar-Annunitum are presumed to hold the administrative and royal records that the provincial finds only reflect. Without the site, accounts of Sargonic administration, art production and the empire's collapse rest on texts from Nippur, Girsu, Adab and other subordinate centres and on later literary traditions such as the Curse of Agade. Its location also fixes the historical geography of the lower Diyala and Tigris and the route network described in Old Babylonian itineraries.
stuck: No inscription naming Agade has been found in situ, and the textual indications (proximity to Sippar, Kish, Eshnunna and the Tigris, a river crossing in Mari itineraries) are compatible with several regions. The Tigris has shifted course since the third millennium, so sites once on its banks may now lie under alluvium, under modern Baghdad or under later occupation. Fieldwork in central Iraq was interrupted for long periods after 1980, and candidate mounds such as Ishan Mizyad and Tell Mohammed have yielded no Sargonic monumental remains.
solved: A ranked list of candidate sites, each scored against every dated textual reference to Agade's position and against reconstructed third-millennium river courses, followed by excavation or coring at the top candidate that recovers Sargonic remains together with inscriptions naming the city or its temple Eulmash.
approach: Research agents can compile every attestation of Agade from the third millennium to the Neo-Babylonian period (royal inscriptions, Mari and Eshnunna letters, itineraries, kudurrus, year names) from CDLI, ORACC and ARCHIBAB, extract distance and direction statements, and test them against GIS reconstructions of palaeochannels traced on CORONA and other declassified imagery.
The output would be a probability surface rather than a single proposal.
Confirmation requires collaboration with Iraqi and international field teams for surface survey, geoarchaeological coring and excavation.

title: How many people lived in the Americas in 1492?
short: Estimates of the hemisphere's population on the eve of contact run from about 8 million to over 100 million, and the scale of the collapse depends on which is right.
matters: The contact population sets the scale of the demographic collapse that followed, and so the magnitude of the most consequential mortality event of the early modern world. It underpins arguments about the density and environmental impact of Indigenous societies (including the extent of anthropogenic landscapes in Amazonia and eastern North America), about the labor economies of the Spanish and Portuguese empires, and about whether reforestation of abandoned land contributed to the atmospheric CO2 minimum around 1610 that Lewis and Maslin proposed as a marker for the Anthropocene.
stuck: Almost no direct counts exist for 1492: early colonial tribute lists, visitas and missionary reports begin decades after epidemics had already struck, so every estimate projects backward through assumed depopulation ratios or carrying capacities. Hemispheric totals are built by summing regional estimates of very uneven quality, and the same sparse figures support results as different as Kroeber's roughly 8.4 million and Dobyns's 90–112 million. Archaeological proxies (settlement counts, radiocarbon date densities, LiDAR-mapped house platforms) measure occupation over centuries rather than population at a single date.
solved: A regional-level reconstruction for c. 1492 in which every region's estimate is tied to an openly published dataset of documentary counts and archaeological proxies, with stated assumptions and uncertainty intervals, such that the hemispheric total and its interval can be recomputed and the main regional disagreements (central Mexico, the Andes, Amazonia, eastern North America) are each narrowed by independent lines of evidence.
approach: AI agents could extract every population figure from digitized tribute rolls, visitas, relaciones geográficas and mission registers into a common table with date, place, unit counted and source, so that depopulation curves can be fitted per province rather than assumed.

This requires further digitization and transcription of tribute and visita series held at the Archivo General de Indias and the Archivo General de la Nación (Mexico) and of Andean visitas and revisitas in Lima and Sucre.

On the archaeological side, collaboration with archaeologists working on LiDAR survey, settlement-pattern data and radiocarbon databases is needed to produce calibrated occupation estimates for the decades just before contact.

title: When was Beowulf composed?
short: Proposed dates for the poem range from about 700 to the early eleventh century, the date of its only manuscript, and rest on metre, language, palaeography and historical context.
matters: An early date (before about 750) makes Beowulf a witness to the culture of Christian Mercia or Northumbria and to oral-traditional material close to the migration period; a date in the Viking age or the reign of Cnut makes it a product of Anglo-Scandinavian politics and late West Saxon literary culture. The choice shapes readings of the poem's attitude to pagan ancestors, Danish kings and Christianity, and its use as evidence for early English legend, Germanic heroic tradition and the history of Old English verse.
stuck: The poem survives in one manuscript copied around 1000, so internal evidence of composition date must be separated from changes introduced by copying. Metrical tests such as Kaluza's law depend on phonological distinctions whose dating and dialect distribution are themselves inferred, and the corpus of securely dated Old English verse is very small. Arguments from palaeographic error patterns, vocabulary and historical allusion each point to a range rather than a date, and scholars weigh them differently.
solved: A dating model trained on Old English texts with independently established dates and transmission histories that assigns Beowulf a composition interval with calibrated uncertainty, and that correctly recovers the known dates of held-out texts, including texts preserved only in late copies.
approach: Agents can build a feature set for every Old English poem and dated prose text from the Dictionary of Old English Corpus and manuscript facsimiles: metrical features (Kaluza's law, contraction, parasite vowels), morphology, vocabulary, spelling layers and scribal error types.
A model calibrated on dated or datable texts, with explicit treatment of copying as a source of noise, can then estimate Beowulf's date and report which features drive it.
All key witnesses are already digitized, so the main need is careful philological annotation that specialists can audit.

title: Did the Black Death reach sub-Saharan Africa in the fourteenth century?
short: Plague devastated Egypt and North Africa in 1347–49, but whether it crossed the Sahara or reached the Horn and East Africa is unresolved.
matters: If plague reached West, East or Northeast Africa, it would offer an explanation for site abandonments, settlement shifts and political reorganizations that archaeologists date to the fourteenth and fifteenth centuries, from the forest zone of southern Ghana to Ife, and it would change how historians read the demographic and political background to the Atlantic encounter. It also bears on the global history of the second pandemic, on whether the Yersinia pestis lineages now endemic in Central and East Africa descend from medieval introductions, and on the long-standing assumption that Africa south of the Sahara was untouched while Eurasia and North Africa lost a large share of their populations.
stuck: Written sources from sub-Saharan Africa for the fourteenth century are few, and Arabic chroniclers who described plague in Egypt and the Maghrib were largely silent about lands beyond the Sahara, a silence that can be read either as absence of plague or absence of reporting. Archaeological signs such as abandonments, mass burials or population decline have other possible causes (drought, war, trade shifts), and few sites are dated precisely enough to tie them to the 1340s–1400s. No medieval Y. pestis genome has yet been published from sub-Saharan Africa, so the genetic argument rests on inferences from the phylogeny of modern African strains.
solved: Recovery of Yersinia pestis DNA, radiocarbon-dated to c. 1340–1500, from human remains at one or more sub-Saharan sites, placed on the second-pandemic phylogeny; or, conversely, systematic negative screening of well-dated fourteenth- and fifteenth-century burials across several regions combined with a full survey of the textual evidence showing no plague references.
approach: AI agents can survey Arabic, Ge'ez, Portuguese and oral-traditional sources for references to epidemic mortality in the fourteenth and fifteenth centuries, including Ethiopian hagiographies and talismanic texts and West African manuscripts now digitized from Timbuktu, and compile a geo-referenced, dated register of candidate sites from the archaeological literature.

Confirmation needs collaboration with ancient-DNA laboratories and African museums and heritage authorities to screen dated burials (for example from Swahili coast towns, the Ethiopian highlands, Nubia and the West African forest and Sahel) for Y. pestis, with radiocarbon dating to fix the chronology, under protocols agreed with descendant communities.

title: How many people lived in China around 1600, and how many died between 1620 and 1680?
short: Late Ming population estimates run from about 150 million to over 200 million, so the scale of the mid-seventeenth-century collapse remains uncertain by tens of millions.
matters: The size of the late Ming population sets the denominator for comparisons of Chinese and European living standards, urbanization and per capita output, including recent historical national accounts. It also determines how catastrophic the Ming–Qing transition was: whether the wars, epidemics and famines of 1620–1680 killed a few tens of millions or a much larger share of the population, and how far the climate-crisis interpretation of the seventeenth century rests on China. Qing-era growth rates, and therefore arguments about the eighteenth-century population boom, depend on where the seventeenth-century trough lay.
stuck: Official Ming registers record roughly 60 million people throughout the dynasty, a figure that reflects fiscal quotas fixed after 1393 rather than headcounts, so every modern total is a reconstruction. Ho Ping-ti (1959) proposed about 150 million for 1600; later work, including Cao Shuji's prefecture-level reconstruction, puts the late Ming peak close to 200 million, with some estimates higher. The central Yellow Register archive in Nanjing was lost, local gazetteer figures vary in what they count, and corrections for under-registration have been applied region by region with assumptions that are hard to compare.
solved: A county- or prefecture-level population series for c.1580, 1630 and 1680 covering at least the core provinces, in which every adjustment to registered figures is stated as an explicit, reproducible rule, and whose implied densities and trends are shown to be consistent with independent evidence on cultivated land, land clearance, grain prices and tax arrears.
approach: Agents can extract every household, ding and mouth figure, land total and tax quota from the digitized Ming and early Qing gazetteers into a single database keyed to CHGIS county boundaries, recording the year and the registration category of each number.

Historians can then specify alternative under-registration models (for example, by ratio of ding to mouths, or by comparison with 1680s Qing registration) and run them consistently across counties, with the agents flagging outliers and internal contradictions for human review.
Cross-checks against grain-price series, reclamation memorials of the 1650s–1680s and local reports of depopulation would test whether a given model produces plausible regional trajectories.
The surviving Yellow Register fragments reused as book-backing paper could provide household-level calibration points if they are systematically imaged and transcribed.

title: How, if at all, did Copernicus learn of the Maragha-school planetary models?
short: Copernicus used devices found earlier in al-Ṭūsī and Ibn al-Shāṭir, but no document shows how a text containing them reached him or his teachers.
matters: If Copernicus drew on the Ṭūsī couple and Ibn al-Shāṭir's lunar and Mercury models, the Copernican revolution sits at the end of a continuous Arabic and Persian reform of Ptolemaic astronomy rather than at a Latin new beginning. The answer bears on how historians describe the relation between Islamic science and the Renaissance, on the role of Byzantine and Jewish intermediaries in fifteenth-century Italy, and on Swerdlow's reconstruction of how Copernicus reached heliocentrism in the first place.
stuck: The mathematical parallels have been clear since Kennedy and Roberts (1959) and Swerdlow and Neugebauer (1984), but Copernicus cites no Arabic author for these devices, and no Latin translation of al-Ṭūsī's Tadhkira or Ibn al-Shāṭir's Nihāyat al-sūl is known. The one securely located carrier, a Ṭūsī-couple diagram in a Byzantine Greek astronomical text in Vat. gr. 211, proves the device reached Italy but not that Copernicus saw it. Skeptics (Di Bono 1995, Blåsjö 2014, 2018) argue that the devices could have been derived independently or from Latin sources such as Proclus, so parallels alone cannot settle the question.
solved: A dated document (a manuscript, annotation, library inventory, loan record or letter) that places a text describing the Ṭūsī couple or Ibn al-Shāṭir's models in the hands of Copernicus, one of his teachers, or a scholar demonstrably in contact with him in Kraków, Bologna, Rome, Padua or Ferrara before about 1514. Alternatively, a documented exhaustive search of the relevant manuscript holdings that finds no such carrier would narrow the hypothesis to independent invention or oral transmission.
approach: Agents can build a census of every Greek, Hebrew, Latin and Arabic manuscript known to contain the Ṭūsī couple or Ibn al-Shāṭir-type models, then cross-reference provenance, ownership marks and library inventories against the prosopography of Copernicus's teachers and Paduan contemporaries such as Amico and Fracastoro, and against Morrison's Jewish intermediaries such as Moses Galeano.

Much of the Vatican, Bodleian and Uppsala material is already online, but progress requires digitizing and cataloguing uncatalogued Hebrew and Greek astronomical miscellanies in Italian, Polish and Central European libraries, and working with curators to read ownership notes and binding evidence.

title: How many people died in the Great Leap Forward famine of 1959–1961?
short: Estimates of excess deaths in China's Great Leap famine range from under 20 million to 45 million, depending on sources, baselines and assumptions about registration.
matters: The death toll is the largest single quantity in the history of the People's Republic and anchors comparative work on twentieth-century famines, state violence and the demography of socialist planning. Economic studies of the famine's causes (procurement, grain exports, communal dining, local political incentives) use the geographic pattern of excess mortality as their dependent variable, so their conclusions inherit any error in that pattern. Long-run studies of fetal and childhood famine exposure also depend on county-level measures of severity.
stuck: The People's Republic has never published an official death count, and the main sources were produced under the same political pressures that caused the famine. Reconstructions from the 1953, 1964 and 1982 censuses and the 1982 One-per-Thousand Fertility Survey gave totals of roughly 23–30 million (Coale, Ashton et al., Banister, Peng Xizhe); later work using county gazetteers and provincial archives produced 32.5 million (Cao Shuji), 36 million (Yang Jisheng) and at least 45 million for 1958–62 (Dikötter), while other authors argue that household-registration catch-up after 1958 inflates recorded deaths and that the true figure is much lower. Estimates differ less over the evidence than over the counterfactual baseline mortality, the treatment of births foregone, migration, and how to correct for deaths registered late.
solved: A published county-level dataset of registered population, births and deaths for 1954–1965 covering all counties with surviving data, with excess-mortality estimates computed under a single stated set of assumptions about baseline mortality and registration error, whose national total reconciles with the 1953, 1964 and 1982 census age structures within stated uncertainty bounds.
approach: Agents can extract annual population, birth and death figures from the post-1980 county gazetteers and provincial statistical compilations into a common table, recording page references and noting where gazetteers revise or contradict one another.

Historians can then fix one set of baseline and registration-correction rules and apply it to every county, report the sensitivity of the total to each assumption, and check the sum against cohort survival in the 1982 census microdata.
Archival series released in the 2000s, including the Song Yongyi document database, can be used to test county figures where both exist.

title: By what route did knowledge of gunpowder reach Latin Europe in the thirteenth century?
short: Gunpowder formulas appear in China by 1044 and in Arabic and Latin texts by the later 1200s, but the path between them is unattested.
matters: The route determines whether gunpowder should be described as a Mongol-era transfer across Eurasia, a product of Mamluk and Andalusian Arabic chemistry, or a partly independent European development from Chinese-derived saltpetre knowledge. It shapes debates over the 'military revolution', over the role of the Mongol empire as a conduit of technology, and over the place of the Islamic world in histories of chemistry and warfare that often move directly from China to Europe.
stuck: The Chinese Wujing zongyao (compiled c. 1040–1044) gives the earliest surviving formulas, but the next datable recipes appear almost simultaneously in the 1260s–1290s in Latin (Roger Bacon's allusions in the Opus maius and Opus tertium, c. 1267; the Liber ignium attributed to Marcus Graecus) and in Arabic (Ḥasan al-Rammāḥ, c. 1270s–1280s), with no text recording a transfer. Arabic terms such as naft and Latin descriptions of incendiaries are ambiguous about whether they mean gunpowder, and the dating of many recipe collections rests on late manuscript copies. Bacon's supposed anagram recipe has been regarded as doubtful since the early twentieth century.
solved: A securely dated text, or a stemma of dated manuscripts, that shows one of the Latin or Arabic gunpowder recipe traditions copying or translating from an identifiable earlier source in another language, so that the direction and approximate date of transfer can be stated. A dated Persian, Arabic or Latin witness of a saltpetre-based recipe earlier than the 1260s outside China would also count.
approach: Agents can assemble a comparative corpus of every dated gunpowder and saltpetre recipe in Chinese, Arabic, Persian, Hebrew and Latin, normalising ingredient proportions, technical vocabulary and purification methods, and then test for textual dependence between traditions.

This requires digitizing and transcribing Arabic and Persian furūsiyya and military manuscripts in Paris, Istanbul, Cairo and elsewhere, and the earliest Latin Liber ignium and Feuerwerkbuch witnesses, with codicologists dating the copies.

title: How did Gutenberg cast his type?
short: Glyph-level variation in the earliest Mainz types has been read both as evidence against the punch, matrix and hand mould, and as fully compatible with it.
matters: The standard account of printing's origin credits Gutenberg with a system of steel punches, copper matrices and an adjustable hand mould, the method that let typefounders produce interchangeable sorts for the next four centuries. If the earliest Mainz types were instead cast from temporary or multiple matrices, the hand mould becomes a later development, possibly from the 1460s, and the chronology of technical invention, the roles of Gutenberg, Fust and Schoeffer, and comparisons with East Asian metal type all need revision. Methods for attributing and dating incunabula from type damage and sort identity also depend on what a 'single sort' is.
stuck: Agüera y Arcas and Needham's computational clustering of the DK type found far more distinct shapes per letter than a single-matrix system should produce, but their full data and methods were only partly published. Critics, above all Reske, argue that inking, paper, pressure, wear and photography generate apparent variation large enough to swamp the signal, so that algorithmic clustering of printed impressions cannot by itself identify matrices. No surviving type, punches or moulds from Gutenberg's shop exist, so the argument rests entirely on inferences from printed impressions.
solved: A published, reproducible dataset of every instance of selected letters across multiple copies of the DK-type prints and the 42-line Bible, with a casting model whose predicted distribution of within-letter variation matches the observed one significantly better than the alternatives, and which is consistent with impressions from experimentally cast type.
approach: Agents can segment and register every glyph instance from the high-resolution digitizations of several B42 copies and the surviving DK-type prints, separating variation that recurs at the same text position across copies (press or inking effects) from variation that recurs across positions (sort identity).

Competing casting processes (single matrix and hand mould, multiple matrices, temporary sand or clay matrices, composite punches) can then be simulated and their predicted variation compared with the observed clusters.

Decisive confirmation would require collaboration with typefounders and materials scientists to cast type by each candidate method, print with period materials, and pass the impressions through the same pipeline.

title: How many people were carried in the Indian Ocean slave trades, 1500–1850?
short: European slave trading in the Indian Ocean has been tentatively counted, but the combined volume of Dutch, Portuguese, French, British, Arab, Swahili and South Asian trades remains unknown.
matters: Without a credible volume, the Indian Ocean cannot be compared with the Atlantic, and claims about the relative weight of African, Malagasy and Asian forced migration in global history rest on guesswork. The numbers bear on the labor regimes of the VOC settlements at Batavia and the Cape, the plantation economies of the Mascarenes, the clove economy of Zanzibar and Pemba, the Gulf pearl industry, and on the demographic history of Madagascar, Mozambique and the East African interior. They also bear on how abolition worked in practice, since the trade shifted to new routes and legal forms after British and French bans.
stuck: There is no voyage-level dataset for the Indian Ocean comparable to the SlaveVoyages trans-Atlantic database, and much of the traffic moved in small numbers aboard ships whose main cargo was something else, so it left little trace in shipping records. The evidence is spread across Dutch, Portuguese, French, English, Arabic, Persian, Gujarati and Swahili sources in archives on four continents, and many local trades (for example within the Indonesian archipelago or along the Swahili coast) were never systematically recorded. Existing estimates either cover only European traders, as in Richard Allen's tentative figure of roughly 570,000 to 730,000 people for 1500–1850, or rest on extrapolations from scattered nineteenth-century observations, as in Ralph Austen's census of the East African trade.
solved: An open, record-level database of documented slave voyages and transfers in the Indian Ocean for 1500–1850, with each record linked to its archival source, from which minimum counts by route, carrier and decade can be computed and gaps quantified, so that a total for all carriers can be stated with an explicit uncertainty range.
approach: AI agents can extract mentions of enslaved people from large digitized series, beginning with the VOC Overgekomen Brieven en Papieren being transcribed by GLOBALISE, Cape and Batavia records, French Mascarene port records and British anti-slave-trade correspondence, and assemble them into voyage and transfer records reviewed by historians.

Progress beyond the Dutch and British material requires new digitization in partnership with the Archives nationales d'outre-mer, the Arquivo Histórico Ultramarino, the National Archives of Mauritius and the Zanzibar National Archives, and with scholars able to read Arabic, Gujarati and Swahili commercial papers.

title: How many Indigenous people were enslaved in the Americas between 1492 and 1900?
short: Andrés Reséndez's estimate of 2.5 to 5 million enslaved Indigenous people is the only hemispheric figure, and it rests on regional extrapolation rather than a count.
matters: The scale of Indigenous enslavement determines how far the demographic collapse of the Americas should be attributed to coerced labor, displacement and violence rather than to epidemic disease alone. It affects the comparison between Indigenous and African slavery in the colonial economies of the Caribbean, Brazil, Chile, northern Mexico, the American Southwest and the English colonies of the Southeast and New England. It also bears on how historians read Spanish and Portuguese abolitions of Indian slavery (1542, 1570, 1755) that were repeatedly evaded through categories such as just war, rescate, encomienda, peonage and 'adoption'.
stuck: Indigenous slavery was frequently illegal or ambiguously legal, so it was recorded under euphemisms (criados, piezas, naborías, administrados, captives) or not recorded at all, and it was dispersed across many small transactions rather than concentrated in shipping. The surviving evidence is scattered among notarial protocols, lawsuits, baptismal registers, probate inventories, military reports and Indigenous testimony in Spanish, Portuguese, French, English and Indigenous languages, mostly undigitized or uncatalogued at item level. Reséndez's 2.5–5 million figure, which he presents as a cautious range, therefore aggregates regional estimates of very different quality, and several regions (Amazonia, the Río de la Plata, Central America after 1550) have no systematic count.
solved: A published, source-linked database of individual enslaved Indigenous people and enslaving events, organized by region and period, from which documented minimums can be computed and combined with explicit, testable multipliers for under-recording, producing a hemispheric range that others can recompute region by region.
approach: AI agents could read digitized notarial protocols, baptismal and burial registers, freedom suits and probate inventories, flag every person described by terms associated with Indigenous bondage, and link repeated appearances of the same individual across record types for historians to review.

The main obstacle is access: progress depends on digitizing and indexing notarial and judicial series in Seville, Mexico City, Santiago de Chile, São Paulo, Lima and Santa Fe in partnership with those archives, and on working with Indigenous communities and projects such as Native Bound Unbound that are already assembling records.

title: Does the Indus script encode language, or a non-linguistic sign system?
short: Whether the short Harappan inscriptions record speech at all has been argued with entropy statistics for two decades; no test yet separates writing from emblem systems decisively.
matters: If the Indus signs are writing, the Harappan civilization was literate and every proposed decipherment (Dravidian, Indo-Aryan, Munda or other) is a legitimate project; if not, it becomes the main case of a large urban society administered without writing, which changes comparative accounts of states and bureaucracy. The answer also governs how seals, tags and pot inscriptions are read as evidence for trade, taxation and identity across a region of perhaps a million square kilometres.
stuck: Inscriptions average about five signs and the longest have only a few dozen, so statistical signatures that distinguish languages from other systems are weak at this length. Farmer, Sproat and Witzel (2004) argued the brevity and sign-repetition patterns are incompatible with writing; Rao et al. (2009) answered that conditional entropy places the corpus within the range of linguistic scripts; Sproat (2010, 2014) showed that several non-linguistic systems also fall in that range. The corpora used by different teams differ in sign lists (roughly 400 to 700 signs) and inclusion rules, and the most complete database (ICIT) requires permission to access.
solved: A pre-registered battery of measures, fixed before the Indus data are scored, classifies a large set of known writing systems and non-linguistic systems (heraldry, mason's marks, deity symbols, administrative codes) correctly when all are trimmed to the Indus length distribution, and then assigns the Indus corpus to one class with stated error rates that are robust to choice of sign list.
approach: Assemble an open, versioned Indus corpus reconciling the Mahadevan, CISI and ICIT sign lists, and build comparison corpora of known scripts and non-linguistic systems sampled to match Indus text lengths, object types and sign inventories, extending Sproat's 2014 dataset.
Fix the classifier and thresholds in a public pre-registration, then report results across alternative sign segmentations.
Progress depends on negotiated open access to ICIT and to the CISI photographic archive, and on recording unpublished excavated material from Pakistan and India.

title: How many died of influenza in India in 1918–19, and why was mortality so high?
short: India probably lost more lives than any other country in the 1918–19 pandemic, but estimates run from about 12 to over 17 million and the causes remain debated.
matters: Because India's toll is the largest single component of every global estimate, the uncertainty there drives much of the spread in estimates of world pandemic mortality, from under 20 million to 50 million or more. The causes of Indian mortality (concurrent drought and food scarcity, wartime prices, malaria, the state of colonial public health, age and sex patterns) are central to arguments about how poverty and governance shape pandemic outcomes and are used to model future pandemics. The demographic shock also figures in the history of Indian nationalism, of the 1921 census 'great divide' in population growth, and of colonial medicine.
stuck: Death registration in British India relied on village watchmen and was incomplete, and the princely states, covering roughly a fifth of the population, kept poorer records or none. Estimates have therefore depended on intercensal comparison, on extrapolation from better-registered provinces, or on assumptions about baseline mortality, which produce different totals. The district-level registers and sanitary reports that would allow finer analysis are held in provincial and state archives and are mostly undigitized.
solved: A district-level panel of registered deaths for 1915–1921 covering all provinces of British India, with a documented correction for under-registration and an imputation for princely states, that yields an all-India excess mortality estimate with uncertainty bounds and identifies the district-level covariates that explain its variation.
approach: Agents can transcribe the printed annual provincial sanitary and vital statistics reports and the 1921 census tables, already partly digitized, into a weekly or monthly district panel, and link them to rainfall, price and food-scarcity series and to malaria returns.
Models of excess mortality can then be tested against independent intercensal estimates.
Extending coverage to the princely states and to sub-district registers requires digitization of holdings in the National Archives of India and state archives, in collaboration with archivists there.

title: How many people were killed in the Irish rising of 1641?
short: Contemporary claims of 154,000 to 300,000 Protestant victims are rejected, but the modern figure of roughly 4,000 killed has never been built from a full victim-level count.
matters: The scale of settler deaths in the winter of 1641–42 shaped English and Scottish policy toward Ireland for a decade, was invoked to justify the Cromwellian conquest and the land confiscations of the 1650s, and remained a fixed point in Protestant and Catholic memory into the twentieth century. Whether the violence amounted to a general massacre, a set of local atrocities, or something in between bears on arguments about colonial violence, sectarian identity, and the comparative history of early modern mass killing. A defensible total, with its distribution in time and place, would also show how far the printed atrocity literature departed from the sworn testimony on which it drew.
stuck: The figures in circulation were produced for polemic: the Lords Justices relayed a claim of 154,000 dead in 1643, Sir John Temple in 1646 wrote of over 300,000 British and Protestants murdered or expelled, and Sir William Petty later proposed about 37,000. Modern estimates, generally around 4,000 killed directly and perhaps 10,000–12,000 including deaths from exposure, hunger and disease, are largely concentrated on Ulster and rest on partial readings rather than a systematic count; Aidan Clarke argued in 2013 that even this consensus needs re-examination. The depositions are dominated by hearsay, the same killings are reported by many deponents with varying names and numbers, and Catholic victims of settler and army reprisals are poorly represented in a source collected from Protestants.
solved: A published, deduplicated database of every death reported in the 1641 Depositions, each linked to the depositions that mention it and coded for eyewitness versus hearsay, place, date and manner, yielding a reproducible minimum count and a stated range for Protestant deaths, with Catholic deaths assessed from other sources.
approach: The full transcription at 1641.tcd.ie and the twelve-volume Irish Manuscripts Commission edition make it feasible for AI agents to extract every reported killing, normalise personal and place names against seventeenth-century gazetteers and the Down Survey, and cluster reports of the same event across depositions.

Historians would set the rules for matching and for weighting hearsay, review uncertain clusters, and cross-check against State Papers, the Ormond correspondence and the 1650s High Court of Justice examinations, then add reprisal killings of Catholics from army and pamphlet sources to give a two-sided total.

title: How many people did the Justinianic Plague kill, and did it change late antique society?
short: Ancient DNA confirms Yersinia pestis caused the First Pandemic (541–c.750), but estimates of its mortality and long-term consequences range from catastrophic to modest.
matters: Maximalist readings make the pandemic a cause of the end of antiquity: depopulation weakening the eastern Roman empire before the Arab conquests, contraction of cities and trade, and the rural and fiscal transformations of the seventh century. Minimalist readings remove that causal link and return explanatory weight to war, climate and political decisions. The answer also shapes comparisons with the Black Death and with modern pandemics, and the use of plague as a general explanation in historical narratives.
stuck: Narrative sources (Procopius, John of Ephesus, Evagrius, Gregory of Tours) give vivid but rhetorically shaped figures for a few cities, and there are almost no serial demographic records. Documentary proxies such as papyri, legislation, coin output, inscriptions and building activity can be read as showing disruption or continuity depending on the baseline chosen. Ancient DNA proves presence of the pathogen at particular sites but not mortality rates, and pollen and settlement data are often too coarse in date to isolate the 540s from other causes.
solved: A region-by-region database of dated proxies (papyri, legislation, coin issues, dated inscriptions, burials with plague DNA, high-resolution pollen cores, settlement and building chronologies) showing, with stated uncertainties, whether measurable discontinuities cluster at the documented plague waves more than expected from a baseline of other shocks, yielding bounded mortality estimates for named regions.
approach: Agents can extract and date every reference to plague waves from narrative and documentary sources, compile counts of dated papyri, inscriptions, laws and coin issues per year and region, and align them with published palaeoecological and aDNA results in a common spatial-temporal framework.
Event-study statistics around each wave, with explicit baselines, would replace selective citation.
Confirmation requires collaboration with ancient-DNA laboratories to screen more burials across the Mediterranean and Near East and with palynologists for well-dated, high-resolution cores.

title: Did Kerala-school infinite series reach early modern Europe through Jesuit missionaries?
short: Madhava's school derived power series for π, sine and cosine before 1500; whether Jesuits in Kerala carried them to Europe remains undocumented.
matters: If Kerala results on infinite series reached Europe, accounts of the origins of the calculus in Gregory, Newton and Leibniz would need to include an Indian component rather than parallel discovery. The question has also become a test case for arguments about the standard of evidence applied to East-to-West versus West-to-East transmission, and for the role of Jesuit colleges as intermediaries in Asian knowledge more generally.
stuck: The Kerala results (attributed to Mādhava, c. 1340–1425, and preserved in Nīlakaṇṭha's Tantrasaṅgraha of 1501 and Jyeṣṭhadeva's Yuktibhāṣā of c. 1530) are securely dated, and Jesuits were present in Cochin from the mid-sixteenth century. But no Jesuit letter, translation, notebook or library record yet produced mentions these series, and Joseph himself reports that a survey of Jesuit literature found no direct trace. The Jesuit college library at Cochin was dispersed when the Dutch took the city in 1663, and relevant Malayalam and Sanskrit manuscripts are scattered and only partly catalogued.
solved: Either a dated document showing a European in possession of, or describing, a Kerala series result before Gregory (1668) and Newton (c. 1665–1669), or a documented, bounded search of the named Jesuit correspondence series (ARSI Goa and Malabar volumes, Documenta Indica, Clavius correspondence) and Kerala manuscript holdings that records the absence of any such reference.
approach: Agents can systematically read the published Documenta Indica and the microfilmed ARSI Goa-Malabar letters for references to Indian astronomy, calendars, Brahmin informants and mathematical manuscripts, and cross-match names of Jesuits in Cochin with correspondents of Clavius and the Collegio Romano.
In parallel they can trace ownership and copying notes in Kerala astronomical manuscripts for European hands.

Progress depends on digitizing the ARSI Goa series at item level and on the Oriental Research Institute and Royal Asiatic Society completing digitization of palm-leaf holdings with searchable catalogues.

title: Do khipus record more than numbers, and can their non-numerical signs be read?
short: Andean knotted cords encode numbers in a known decimal system; whether colour, ply, attachment and knot direction also record names, categories or narrative remains open.
matters: Colonial chroniclers reported that khipukamayuq read histories, genealogies and laws from cords. If khipus encoded non-numerical information systematically, the Inka state kept records that could be read as primary sources for Andean history before and after 1532, and the comparative history of writing would need to include a non-graphic system. If they did not, accounts of Inka administration must explain how a large empire functioned on numerical records plus memory.
stuck: Roughly a thousand khipus survive (estimates vary), most without archaeological context, and very few can be paired with a Spanish-language transcription of the same record. The decimal knot system was established by Locke (1912) and the Aschers, but colour, fibre, spin and ply, attachment direction and knot orientation vary in ways that have resisted consistent interpretation. Data were long scattered across incompatible recording schemes and unpublished notebooks.
solved: A model trained on matched khipu–document pairs predicts, for khipus or transcriptions held out from training, non-numerical features (such as moiety, lineage, place or personal-name categories) significantly better than chance and better than numerical-only baselines, and the predictions are confirmed when new matched pairs are found.
approach: Use the Open Khipu Repository and Khipu Field Guide as a common schema, and systematically search colonial visitas, revisitas and court records in Peruvian and Spanish archives for documents stating that their figures were read from khipus, then match them by totals and structure as Medrano and Urton did for the Santa Valley khipus.
Test competing readings, such as the alternative moiety alignments of Medrano and Urton (2018) and FitzPatrick (2024), against held-out cord groups.

This depends on recording undocumented khipus in museum stores, especially in Berlin, Lima and smaller Peruvian collections, and on community agreements for khipus still held in villages such as Collata and Rapaz.

title: What language does Linear A record, and can any proposed family beat chance?
short: Minoan Linear A can be roughly sounded out through Linear B values, but no proposed language family has been shown to fit better than random controls.
matters: The language of Linear A bears on who the Minoans were, how Bronze Age Crete related to Anatolia, the Levant and Egypt, and what the Mycenaean Greeks inherited when they adapted the script as Linear B. Readings of personal names, toponyms and religious formulae on libation vessels would change accounts of Minoan religion and administration. A demonstration that no candidate family is detectable at this corpus size would also be a result, setting limits on what further comparative claims can mean.
stuck: The corpus is small and mostly administrative: about 1,430 documents in the original GORILA edition and 1,534 after the 2024–25 supplement, most of them short tallies, sealings and roundels, with roughly 7,500 signs in all. Linear B values give approximate pronunciations, but the transfer of values is itself an assumption, and many proposals (Luwian, Semitic, Hurrian, Tyrsenian and others) have been argued by selective lexical matching without controls for how many matches chance would produce. Few proposals have been stated in advance in a form that could fail.
solved: A language-family hypothesis, specified before testing (sound correspondences, morphology, lexicon), predicts readings of held-out inscriptions significantly better than the same procedure applied to shuffled sign values and unrelated control languages; or a power analysis shows that no such test can succeed at the current corpus size. A narrower solvable target is a complete, consistent account of the fraction signs and commodity totals (KU-RO) that balances the surviving tallies.
approach: Build a machine-readable corpus from SigLA, lineara.xyz and the GORILA supplement, with transliteration uncertainty encoded per sign.

title: How many early printed editions have been lost without trace?
short: Estimates of the share of fifteenth- and sixteenth-century editions that survive in no copy vary widely, and depend on statistical models that have rarely been tested against later discoveries.
matters: Quantitative histories of the early book trade, of literacy and of the spread of ideas count surviving editions as if they were a fixed fraction of what was printed. If loss was heavy and uneven, falling hardest on cheap, small-format, vernacular, ephemeral and heavily used books such as schoolbooks, almanacs, broadsides and devotional texts, then the apparent dominance of Latin learned printing and the relative output of regions and printers are artefacts of survival. The same estimates are used to calibrate long-run series of book production that feed into economic history.
stuck: Lost editions leave evidence only indirectly, in booksellers' catalogues, inventories, references, binding fragments and editions known from a single copy. Statistical estimates depend on assumptions about how copy counts are distributed, and the main models give different answers for different categories of book. Catalogues such as ISTC, GW and USTC are revised continuously, but no one has systematically used their revision history to test whether past estimates correctly predicted the rate and kind of new discoveries.
solved: A survival model fitted on a dated snapshot of a major catalogue (for example ISTC or USTC as of a past year) that correctly predicts the number and category distribution of editions added in later years, together with an estimate of total lost editions by format, language and genre with stated uncertainty.
approach: Agents can reconstruct historical states of ISTC, GW, USTC and VD16 from published versions, data exports and change logs, record copy counts per edition, and fit unseen-species estimators (Chao1, Efron–Thisted and successors) separately for format, language and genre.

Predictions from older snapshots can then be scored against editions discovered since, and the documentary record of lost books (booksellers' lists, inventories, privileges) used as an independent check.
All the needed catalogues are already online, so no new digitization is required, though cooperation with catalogue maintainers would allow access to dated record histories.

title: Were Mendel's pea-hybrid data too close to expectation, and if so, why?
short: Fisher showed in 1936 that Mendel's ratios fit theory improbably well; a century of explanations has not produced documentary evidence of how the counts were made.
matters: Mendel's paper is the founding document of genetics and a standard case in teaching about scientific integrity, so whether his numbers were selected, adjusted, unconsciously biased or simply lucky affects how the episode is taught and how historians read his intentions. The answer also bears on what Mendel set out to do, whether he tested a pre-formed theory or reported plant-breeding experiments, and on the reception of his work by Nägeli and the rediscoverers of 1900.
stuck: Fisher's chi-square analysis found an overall fit with a probability of roughly 7 in 100,000 and also argued that Mendel's 2:1 ratios in the progeny tests should have been biased toward 1.7:1. Mendel's experimental notebooks do not survive, and many of his papers are reported to have been burned after his death in 1884, so only the published paper and a handful of letters to Nägeli constrain explanations. Proposed solutions (a too-eager assistant, sequential stopping, selective reporting, a different sampling model, botanical factors such as pollen tetrads) are each compatible with the summary numbers and therefore hard to discriminate.
solved: Either discovery of primary records (field notes, seed counts, or correspondence) that show how Mendel collected and selected his counts, or a statistical analysis that specifies a historically documented procedure and shows that it reproduces both Fisher's goodness-of-fit anomaly and the 2:1 progeny-test anomaly at conventional significance, while competing procedures do not.
approach: Agents can encode every count in the 1866 paper and the Nägeli letters, reproduce the main published statistical models (Fisher, Edwards, Pires and Branco and others) in a single framework, and test which assumptions each depends on.

They can also search monastery, school, horticultural society and Brno natural-history society records for references to Mendel's assistants, seed exchanges and garden practice, and search the papers of Nägeli and other correspondents for unpublished material.

title: Can the Meroitic language be translated beyond its funerary formulae?
short: Meroitic script has been readable since Griffith's work of 1909–1911, but outside formulaic texts the language of the Kingdom of Kush is still largely untranslated.
matters: Meroitic is the oldest written language of sub-Saharan Africa and the administrative and royal language of Kush for some seven centuries. The long royal stelae, temple texts and chronicles almost certainly record wars with Rome, succession and religious practice from a Kushite point of view; at present historians rely on Greek, Latin and Egyptian sources for that history. A secure classification would also date the spread of Northern East Sudanic languages along the Nile, which bears on Nubian linguistic and population history.
stuck: The script's sound values were recovered from Egyptian names, but there is no substantial bilingual text, and the language has no close, well-documented descendant. Most of the corpus consists of funerary inscriptions with predictable formulae, so the vocabulary securely understood is small, by most accounts on the order of a hundred words, and grammar is reconstructed mainly from those formulae. Classification is disputed: Rilly argues for the Northern East Sudanic branch with Nubian, Nara, Taman and Nyima, while Rowan and Lipiński have argued for an Afroasiatic affiliation.
solved: A lexicon and grammar, fixed before testing, yield translations of held-out non-funerary passages (for example sections of royal stelae or temple texts) that independent specialists judge consistent with their archaeological, iconographic and historical context, and that correctly predict content later confirmed by newly found or newly published inscriptions.
approach: Convert the REM corpus and inscriptions published since 2000 into a machine-readable, lemmatized corpus with find context, object type and date.

Use reconstructed Proto-Northern East Sudanic and Old Nubian vocabulary to generate constrained translation hypotheses, and test them against held-out passages whose context (offering scenes, lists of places, military iconography) predicts parts of the content.

Comparative work needs collaboration with Nubian and Nilo-Saharan linguists, and the corpus needs digitization of inscriptions excavated after 2000 and photographs held by excavation missions, given reported damage to collections in Khartoum during the war that began in 2023.

title: What is the absolute chronology of early second-millennium BCE Mesopotamia?
short: Competing High, Middle, Low and Ultra-Low chronologies place Hammurabi and the fall of Babylon up to about 150 years apart; no single model integrates all the evidence.
matters: The relative sequence of Old Assyrian, Old Babylonian and Kassite rulers is well established, but its anchor in absolute years is not, so every date before about 1400 BCE in Mesopotamia, Anatolia, Syria and the Levant inherits the uncertainty. Synchronisms with Egypt, the Hittite sack of Babylon, the dating of the Santorini eruption debate, climate-and-collapse arguments and comparisons with radiocarbon-dated archaeology all depend on which option is chosen. The four usual options put the fall of Babylon at 1651, 1595, 1531 or 1499 BCE.
stuck: The Venus observations preserved in later copies of Enūma Anu Enlil tablet 63 are corrupt and allow several solutions roughly 56 or 64 years apart, and month-length and eclipse arguments depend on contested readings and observational assumptions. Assyrian King List distance figures contain uncertain reign lengths, and the Kültepe eponym lists must be joined to Old Babylonian sources through a small number of synchronisms. Dendrochronological sequences from Anatolian sites were long only floating, and their wiggle-matched radiocarbon dates carry their own calibration and regional-offset uncertainties.
solved: A published, reproducible Bayesian model that ingests the Venus data, lunar month lengths, eclipse candidates, king-list and eponym-list distance numbers, dendrochronological sequences and radiocarbon dates with explicit priors, returns a posterior for a fixed anchor (such as Ammisaduqa year 1) with a stated uncertainty under 10 years, and remains stable when individual lines of evidence are removed.
approach: Agents can build a machine-readable dataset of every chronologically relevant datum (each Venus copy and its variant readings, month-length records from Old Babylonian archives, eponym-list entries, reign lengths, synchronisms) with full citations, then encode them as constraints in a radiocarbon-modelling framework such as OxCal.
Sensitivity analysis would show which items drive the result.

New radiocarbon and dendrochronological measurements on securely contexted short-lived samples and timbers from Kültepe, Acemhöyük and Babylonian sites require collaboration with dendrochronology and radiocarbon laboratories.

title: Did the population of Ottoman Anatolia collapse in the late sixteenth and seventeenth centuries?
short: Tax surveys show rapid growth in Anatolia to about 1580, but whether the decline that followed was a demographic collapse or an artefact of changing registration remains unsettled.
matters: A large fall in Anatolian population would connect the Celali rebellions, the Little Ice Age droughts of the 1590s, rural flight and the transformation of Ottoman fiscal and military institutions into one crisis comparable to the 'general crisis' of seventeenth-century Europe and China. If the decline was smaller or mainly a shift from registered villages to towns, nomadism and untaxed settlements, then narratives of Ottoman 'decline' and of climate-driven collapse need revision. The question also tests whether Ottoman tax registers can be used for demography at all.
stuck: The detailed provincial surveys (tahrir defterleri) end in most of Anatolia by the 1580s and record taxable household heads rather than people, while the seventeenth-century avarız and cizye registers that follow count fiscal units (avarızhane) whose relation to households changed over time. Comparisons across the two series therefore mix demographic change with changes in what was counted. Most studies cover single districts, the registers are held in two archives with different access regimes, and many have never been transcribed.
solved: A linked village-level dataset across all surviving tahrir and avarız registers for a large sample of Anatolian districts, with a validated model converting each register's fiscal units into households, that produces regional population series from 1520 to 1700 with uncertainty and that agrees with independent evidence such as court records, settlement abandonment and cizye counts.
approach: Agents can help transcribe and structure registers from facsimiles and published editions, match village names across registers and to modern locations, and estimate conversion factors between fiscal units and households where registers overlap.
Regional series could then be tested against climate reconstructions, Celali violence and court-record evidence of flight.

Scaling beyond published registers requires systematic digitization of the Tapu Tahrir (TT.d) and avarız series in the Ottoman Archives in Istanbul and the Kuyûd-ı Kadîme registers in Ankara, with collaboration from archivists and Ottoman palaeographers, since many registers use siyakat numerals and chancery hands that need specialist verification.

title: Does Proto-Elamite record language, and is it the ancestor of Linear Elamite?
short: Iran's earliest script survives on about 1,600–1,700 accounting tablets; its numbers are read, but whether its other signs write words, and how it relates to Linear Elamite, is disputed.
matters: Proto-Elamite is one of the earliest scripts anywhere and the first on the Iranian plateau, so its nature bears on whether writing was invented once in Mesopotamia and borrowed, or developed independently in more than one place. If its non-numerical signs encode syllables of Elamite, the history of that language extends back almost a millennium. Desset and colleagues' 2022 decipherment of Linear Elamite rests partly on a claimed continuity from Proto-Elamite; whether that continuity holds affects how far the decipherment can be pushed back.
stuck: The tablets are almost all administrative accounts from Susa, with smaller groups from Tepe Yahya, Tal-i Malyan, Tepe Sofalin and other sites; they contain several hundred non-numerical signs and short entries dominated by numbers. The numerical systems were largely worked out by Damerow and Englund through comparison with Mesopotamian proto-cuneiform, but the remaining signs could be logograms, personal names, institutional labels or syllables, and the short entries offer few repeated phonetic contexts. More than five centuries separate the last Proto-Elamite tablets from the first Linear Elamite inscriptions, and Dahl (2023) argues that Linear Elamite was a deliberate new creation rather than a descendant.
solved: A structural analysis that partitions the sign inventory into numerical, logographic and candidate phonetic signs, with stated criteria, is validated on proto-cuneiform where the answers are known; applied to Proto-Elamite, it either identifies a set of signs whose distribution fits a syllabary, with predicted values that cohere with Linear Elamite readings beyond chance, or shows that no such subset exists.
approach: Start from the CDLI transliterations and images, and treat the numerical layer as a solved constraint system so that every tablet's arithmetic is checked and the residual signs isolated.

Train sign-distribution models on proto-cuneiform and early cuneiform, where logograms, determinatives and phonetic complements are known, then test whether Proto-Elamite contains a comparable phonetic subset, following the computational work of Born, Kelley and colleagues.
Test the claimed Linear Elamite relation with pre-registered sign-form and value correspondences against shuffled pairings.
Unpublished and poorly imaged tablets in the Louvre and in Iranian collections need high-resolution imaging, which requires collaboration with those institutions.

title: Did Ptolemy observe the Almagest star catalogue or adapt Hipparchus's?
short: Ptolemy's catalogue of about 1,025 stars claims his own observations; statistical anomalies suggest much of it derives from Hipparchus three centuries earlier.
matters: The Almagest catalogue is the oldest fully preserved star catalogue and the basis of Western and Islamic stellar astronomy until Ulugh Beg. Whether it records new observations bears on Ptolemy's reliability as a witness to his own practice, on the reconstruction of Hipparchus's lost catalogue, on the value of ancient positions for measuring precession and proper motion, and on broader arguments about how ancient scientists used data.
stuck: Ptolemy dates the catalogue to the first year of Antoninus (AD 137) and implies he observed it, but its longitudes are systematically about 1° too small for that date, consistent with adding a precession of 1° per century to positions for Hipparchus's epoch. Statistical tests of epoch, observer latitude, rounding patterns and error structure have yielded conflicting verdicts because the catalogue may mix sources and because results depend on modelling choices. Until 2022 there were almost no direct Hipparchan coordinates against which to compare.
solved: Recovery of enough of Hipparchus's own coordinates (from palimpsests or other witnesses) to show for a substantial sample of stars whether Ptolemy's entries equal Hipparchan values shifted by 2°40′ in longitude, or differ in ways that require independent measurement; or a pre-registered statistical analysis of the whole catalogue, using modern astrometry, that discriminates between the two hypotheses for defined subsets of stars.
approach: Agents can rebuild the competing statistical tests from a single machine-readable edition of the catalogue and modern Hipparcos and Gaia positions, making every assumption explicit and reporting results by constellation and source subset.
In parallel, they can systematically compare newly recovered Hipparchan readings with Ptolemy's entries.

Further progress depends on multispectral imaging of the remaining undertext of the Codex Climaci Rescriptus and other Sinai palimpsests by imaging scientists, and on collaboration with astronomers to model proper motion and refraction.

title: How literate was the population of late imperial China?
short: Rawski's 1979 estimate of 30–45 percent male literacy in Qing China has never been tested against a systematic count of signatures and marks on contracts.
matters: Literacy levels underpin arguments about Qing commercial capacity, the reach of print and vernacular fiction, popular religion and sectarian movements, and the state's ability to govern through written documents. Comparative economic history uses Chinese human capital in debates over the Great Divergence, and the claim that the character script did not hold back mass literacy rests largely on Rawski's figures. Estimates of women's literacy shape histories of gender and household management.
stuck: Rawski's range (roughly 30–45 percent of men and 2–10 percent of women with some reading ability) was inferred from school provision, the price and circulation of primers, and observers' impressions rather than from a direct measure. Literacy in China was graded and functional, so a single threshold is hard to define, and scholars since have favoured qualitative studies of 'literacies' over counts. Contracts survive in the hundreds of thousands, but most were written by scribes (daibi) and bear marks, crosses or signatures whose meaning has not been coded systematically, and the published facsimile series are scattered across regions with very different social structures.
solved: A coded sample of at least several thousand Qing contracts from more than one region, recording for each named party and witness whether they wrote their own name, wrote it in a different hand from the scribe, or made a mark, with the proportion of autograph signatures reported by decade, region, sex and role, and an explicit argument for how that proportion relates to reading ability.
approach: Agents can work through published facsimile series (the Huizhou sets, Qingshui River manuscripts, Taiwan land deeds) to locate the signature block of each contract, classify each party's subscription as autograph, scribe-written or mark, and record the scribe's name so that the same hand can be recognised across documents; historians would verify a random subsample by eye.
The method follows Cressy's English signature counts, but the coding rules must be adapted to Chinese practice, where scribes routinely wrote parties' names and parties added a hua ya mark.
Digitization is needed because many contract holdings in county archives and university collections are catalogued but not imaged, and those that are imaged are often not publicly accessible.

title: When was the consonantal text of the Qurʾān standardized?
short: Islamic tradition credits the caliph ʿUthmān (c. 650); some scholars place closure under ʿAbd al-Malik and al-Ḥajjāj (c. 700) or later. Manuscript evidence is now testing these positions.
matters: The date at which the consonantal skeleton (rasm) was fixed determines how far the text can be used as evidence for the first decades of Islam, how its relation to Muhammad's preaching is assessed, and how the early caliphate's religious authority is understood. A mid-seventh-century closure supports reading the Qurʾān as a near-contemporary witness; a Marwanid or later closure would allow for substantial editorial shaping during the conquest period. The question also bears on the history of Arabic orthography and on the reliability of the Islamic tradition's accounts of collection.
stuck: The earliest manuscripts are fragmentary, undated, dispersed across collections and often published only in part, and the Sanaa lower text survives as an erased palimpsest. Radiocarbon dates give the death of the animal whose skin became parchment, not the date of writing, and their ranges often span several decades on either side of 650 and 700. The literary accounts of ʿUthmān's and al-Ḥajjāj's interventions were recorded later and are read differently by scholars with different views of the tradition's reliability.

title: How large was the Roman citizen population in the late Republic and under Augustus?
short: Roman census totals jump from about 910,000 in 70/69 BCE to 4,063,000 in 28 BCE; whether this reflects a change in who was counted or real growth remains disputed.
matters: Estimates of Italy's population under Augustus range from roughly 5–7 million on the low count to 14 million or more on the high count, and every account of late Republican agrarian crisis, slavery, military recruitment, urbanization, colonization and per-capita income in Roman Italy builds on one of them. The low count implies a stagnant or declining free rural population consistent with the Gracchan narrative of peasant displacement; the high count implies substantial growth and a densely settled countryside. The figures are also a benchmark for population estimates of the whole empire.
stuck: The surviving totals are bare numbers transmitted by literary sources (Livy's Periochae, Phlegon of Tralles, Augustus' Res Gestae) with no statement of who was registered, and the text tradition itself varies (the Periocha for 70/69 BCE is transmitted as 900,000, Phlegon gives 910,000, and the Greek version of the Res Gestae differs from the Latin for 28 BCE). The 70/69 BCE figure is widely thought to be an undercount after the Social War enfranchisement, so the size of the jump is itself uncertain. Survey archaeology, the main independent check, depends on site-recovery rates, dating of surface ceramics and assumptions about household size that are hard to calibrate.
solved: A model that converts each reading (low, middle, high) into predicted densities of occupied rural sites and urban areas for specific surveyed regions, compared against harmonized survey datasets with stated recovery rates, showing that one reading fits the observed settlement record within its uncertainty and the others do not.
approach: Agents can assemble all census figures with their textual variants, enfranchisement and colonization data and the main demographic models into one dataset, then harmonize published field-survey gazetteers (Tiber Valley, Roman Suburbium, Pontine Region, Albegna/Ager Cosanus, Biferno and others) into site counts by period and size class.
Bayesian estimation of recovery rates across overlapping surveys would let the competing counts be scored against the same evidence.

Progress needs digitization of legacy survey archives and site cards held by the British School at Rome and Italian and Dutch institutions, in collaboration with their archivists and survey directors.

title: How much American silver reached China between 1550 and 1800?
short: Estimates of the share of Spanish American silver that ended up in China vary widely because mint, shipping and Chinese monetary records have never been reconciled in one account.
matters: The volume of silver entering China is central to the argument that world trade became global after the founding of Manila in 1571, to explanations of the Ming fiscal shift to silver, and to debates over whether a contraction of silver imports helped bring down the Ming in the 1630s–40s. It also bears on European price history, on the Dutch and English East India Companies' balance of trade, and on nineteenth-century arguments that the reversal of silver flows destabilised the Qing.
stuck: Silver reached China by several routes (the Manila galleons, the Cape route via European companies, overland through Central Asia, and from Japan, which was a larger supplier than the Americas for parts of the period), and each route is documented in different archives with different biases. Registered mint and treasury output understates production because of contraband and unregistered silver, and smuggling on the Acapulco–Manila route was extensive. Chinese sources record taxes, prices and exchange rates rather than imports, so arrivals must be inferred, and published estimates (Barrett, Flynn and Giráldez, von Glahn, TePaske) rest on different assumptions about leakage, re-export and Japanese supply.
solved: A route-by-route, decade-by-decade mass balance for 1550–1800 in which American registered production plus an explicit contraband estimate equals the sum of silver retained in the Americas, shipped to Europe, re-exported to Asia, and carried across the Pacific, with China's share derived from these flows and checked against Japanese exports and Chinese monetary indicators (silver–copper exchange rates, tax receipts in silver, price levels).
approach: Agents can assemble the published quantitative series (TePaske's mint and treasury data, Garner's mining series, VOC and East India Company bullion exports, galleon registers, Japanese export estimates) into one linked dataset with source citations and documented units, then flag gaps and double counting between routes.

Historians can specify alternative contraband and re-export assumptions and see how each changes the China total, while agents search the AGI, AGN and VOC finding aids for unused series (for example Manila customs and Acapulco registers) that would narrow the largest uncertainties.
Chinese provincial price and exchange-rate data from the Qing archives provide an independent test of the timing of inflows.

title: How much iron did Song China produce in the eleventh century?
short: Robert Hartwell's estimate of about 125,000 tons of iron in 1078 is widely repeated, but it rests on fiscal records whose relation to total output is disputed.
matters: Hartwell's figure is the main quantitative support for the idea of a Northern Song 'industrial revolution' and for claims that Chinese iron output in 1078 rivalled that of Britain in the late eighteenth century. It is used in world histories, in comparative arguments about the Great Divergence, and in environmental histories of deforestation and the shift from charcoal to coal. If output was much lower, or largely charcoal-fuelled, the narrative of a Song coal-and-iron breakthrough that later stalled needs revision.
stuck: The figure is extrapolated from iron receipts recorded for state monopoly and tax purposes in compilations such as the Song huiyao and Wenxian tongkao, which record what the state collected, not what was produced, and Hartwell's multiplier from receipts to output is an assumption. Donald Wagner argued that these administrative figures cannot be scaled up so simply, and Tim Wright's review of four decades of citation found that the estimate has been repeated far more often than tested. Archaeological evidence for Song ironworks is patchy: few smelting sites have been excavated and published in detail, and slag volumes, furnace capacities and fuel types have not been surveyed systematically.
solved: An output estimate for the 1070s, with explicit error bounds, built from at least two independent lines of evidence (the fiscal record re-read prefecture by prefecture with a stated model of collection rates, and archaeological slag-heap volumes and furnace capacities from surveyed sites), with the two lines agreeing within their stated uncertainties.
approach: Agents can extract every reference to iron production sites (ye, jian, wu), quotas and receipts from the full-text Song huiyao jigao, Xu zizhi tongjian changbian, Wenxian tongkao and Song gazetteers, map them to prefectures and dates, and assemble the competing readings of how quotas related to production.
Historians can then compare alternative collection-rate models in a single framework.

Confirmation requires collaboration with archaeometallurgists: systematic survey and volumetric measurement of slag heaps at known Song iron districts (for example around Handan and Cizhou in Hebei, and in Shanxi and Henan), radiocarbon dating of charcoal and coke inclusions, and analysis of slag and cast-iron objects (sulphur content and other tracers) to separate charcoal-fired from coal-fired production.

title: Did Vermeer use a camera obscura or other optical aids?
short: Optical effects, perspective geometry and technical imaging have been read for and against Vermeer's use of a camera obscura, with no documentary evidence either way.
matters: Vermeer is the test case for broader claims that optical projection shaped European naturalism, including the Hockney–Falco thesis, and for how far seventeenth-century Dutch painting drew on contemporary optics in Delft, the city of Leeuwenhoek. The answer bears on how his paintings were made (tracing, transfer or free construction), on attributions and chronology based on technique, and on whether instruments such as the camera obscura were working tools for painters or mainly objects of natural-philosophical interest.
stuck: No document records Vermeer owning or using an optical device, and the 1676 inventory of his household lists none. The visual evidence (halation, differential focus, perspective and scale relationships) is compatible with optical observation but can also be produced by skilled painting, and proponents and critics have relied on different paintings and different reconstructions. Recent technical imaging has shown underpainting and revisions that complicate any model of direct tracing without settling whether projection was used at some stage.
solved: A quantitative model of the geometry, scale and focus effects predicted by specific optical set-ups in a reconstructed studio, tested across all securely attributed paintings and against their underdrawings and pinhole evidence, that either fits significantly better than free-hand construction with a pin-and-string perspective or is shown to add no explanatory power.
approach: Agents can assemble a structured corpus of Vermeer's paintings with published technical imaging (infrared reflectography, MA-XRF, X-radiography, pinhole locations), extract perspective lines, object sizes and focus gradients, and test them against simulated projections from the room geometries reconstructed by Steadman and others.
A parallel search of Delft notarial, guild and Jesuit records, and of optical literature circulating in the Dutch Republic, could look for documentary links.
Confirmation needs collaboration with museum conservation scientists for access to full-resolution technical datasets and with optical engineers for physical reconstructions.

existing.title: Traces of Vermeer
existing.note: A painter's experimental reconstruction proposing that Vermeer traced projected images onto oiled paper and transferred them as monochrome underpaintings.

existing.authors: Abbie Vandivere, Annelies van Loon, Kathryn A. Dooley, Ralph Haswell, Robert G. Erdmann, Emilien Leonhardt
existing.title: Revealing the painterly technique beneath the surface of Vermeer's Girl with a Pearl Earring using macro- and microscale imaging
existing.note: Girl in the Spotlight project (Mauritshuis, 2018): imaging identified ground, fine black outlines and underlayers, evidence for the sequence of construction against which tracing hypotheses can be tested.

existing.authors: David G. Stork, Christopher W. Tyler and Sara J. Schechner
existing.title: Did Tim Paint a Vermeer?
existing.venue: Journal of Imaging Science and Technology 64 (6): 060403
existing.note: Critique of Tim Jenison's mirror-comparator method shown in Teller's film Tim's Vermeer (2013), concluding that Vermeer was very unlikely to have used it.

existing.title: Johannes Vermeer: Faith, Light and Reflection
existing.note: Published with the 2023 Rijksmuseum exhibition; links Vermeer's optical effects to Jesuit interest in the camera obscura in Delft, an interpretive argument without direct documentary proof.

archives.collection: Girl with a Pearl Earring and View of Delft; technical data from The Girl in the Spotlight (2018)
archives.note: Project results are summarized online and published in Heritage Science; full scan datasets require request to the museum.

archives.note: High-resolution images are open access; the 2022 Milkmaid study revealed an underpainting and painted-out jug holder and fire basket.

archives.collection: Lady at the Virginals with a Gentleman ('The Music Lesson'), RCIN 405346
archives.note: The painting at the centre of Steadman's room reconstruction and of Jenison's replication.
